title: Which earlier characters might help?
body: Part I predicted the next character in a name such as aabid. The question stays the same; we are changing how the model reads the known context.

title: Back to the river bank
body: One query can benefit from several clues at once. What setting are we in? Who is there?

title: Keep the two examples separate
body: The worksheet explains the arithmetic. Held-out results later tell us whether the trained models improved.

title: From one weight row to two
body: What changes when the same input passes through two sets of projections?

title: One head produces one message
body: One head can already read several sources. Its value coordinates share the same attention weights.

title: Two heads keep two messages
body: Each head has its own Q, K and V projections and its own softmax. Both receive the full E.

title: Project first; split the projected coordinates
body: We split Q, K and V after projection. We do not give head 1 the first half of the raw embedding and head 2 the second half.

title: Separate heads can use different input features
body: These are two 4×2 matrices placed side by side. Every head can learn from every input coordinate.

title: Two heads, one receiving token
body: Keep the final “the” at position 10 as the query throughout.

title: Start with the same position-aware rows
body: E already includes token embedding + position embedding. Token IDs are not embedding coordinates.

title: The first query asks about the setting
body: Our chosen projection copies the glue coordinate into both query coordinates: [2.3, 2.3].

title: The second query uses a different projection
body: The same input row now produces [2.3, 0.0]. The query changes because the projection matrix changes.

title: The source keys are different too
body: Head 1 exposes water/finance features. Head 2 exposes person/glue features. These labels belong to this designed worksheet.

title: Head 1 scores the river key
body: The scaling uses the head width: two coordinates, not four.

title: Head 2 scores the fisherman key
body: We compare each head’s query only with keys from that same head.

title: Head 1: scores become a weight row
body: Each weight is exp(score) divided by the sum of exp(scores) in this row. All ten sources are allowed for the final query.

title: Head 2 has its own softmax
body: Normalize over sources within head 2. Do not normalize across heads or average their scores.

title: Head 1 sends water and finance information
body: The river contribution is its weight × its value row. Add the contributions from every source to get the two-coordinate message.

title: Head 2 sends a different kind of message
body: The second head mixes its own values with its own weights. Matching features choose where to read; values carry the information.

title: Bring the two messages back together
body: How do two small message rows become one update to the original row?

title: Concatenate the messages, not the tokens
body: Two 2-coordinate rows become one 4-coordinate row. Concatenation preserves both feature groups; it does not average them.

title: W_O can mix information across heads
body: Water update = 2.617 + 0.25 × 1.552 = 3.005. W_O maps the joined message back to model width.

title: Add the update to the original row
body: The residual is the same addition as in Part II. There is still one updated row per input token.

title: The prediction MLP stays in place
body: Choose a token only after vocabulary softmax. Attention weights choose source positions; vocabulary probabilities choose possible next tokens.

title: Change the context; inspect both heads
From the drawing to tensors
body: Keep B = 2 examples, T = 10 tokens, D = 4 coordinates and H = 2 heads.

title: Create the tables, projections and prediction MLP
body: The download defines every layer. Load the hand-chosen worksheet weights to reproduce the printed numbers; ordinary training starts from random parameters.
code:
model = TinyMultiHeadLM(vocab_size=20, context=10,
                        width=4, heads=2, hidden=8)
load_worksheet_weights(model, worksheet)

title: Two input windows form one batch
body: These are integer IDs, not embeddings. Each example has one observed target.
code:
X = torch.tensor([river_ids, cheque_ids])
y = torch.tensor([word_to_id["water"], word_to_id["teller"]])

title: Find the embedding lookup on the map
body: We have token IDs. Next, look up their learned rows and add the position rows. Both heads will read the result.

title: Look up token rows and add position rows
body: The embedding tables are learned parameters. E contains floating-point vectors with shape [2,10,4].

title: Project the full input three times
body: Different learned matrices give matching queries, matching keys and transmitted values.
code:
Q = model.attention.W_Q(E)
K = model.attention.W_K(E)
V = model.attention.W_V(E)

title: Make the head axis explicit
body: reshape groups projected coordinates; transpose puts heads before tokens. Apply the same operation to K and V.
code:
Q = Q.reshape(2, 10, 2, 2).transpose(1, 2)
K = K.reshape(2, 10, 2, 2).transpose(1, 2)
V = V.reshape(2, 10, 2, 2).transpose(1, 2)

title: Compute every query–key pair within each head
body: The first two axes keep examples and heads separate. Matrix multiplication contracts only the matching-coordinate axis.
code:
scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)
scores = scores / math.sqrt(2)

title: Block future sources in every head
body: True marks a blocked entry. The same causal mask broadcasts across both examples and both heads.
code:
future = torch.ones(10, 10, dtype=torch.bool).triu(1)
scores = scores.masked_fill(future, float("-inf"))

title: Each row becomes a distribution over sources
body: The final axis indexes source tokens. Every allowed row sums to one; masked entries have weight zero.

title: Multiply the weights by the values
body: The source-token axis is summed out. Each head keeps its own two-coordinate message.

title: Put each token’s head messages side by side
body: Transpose before reshaping. A direct reshape of the original layout would mix token rows with head rows.

title: Return to the shared prediction path
body: The two head messages are joined. W_O mixes them, and the residual adds that update to the original E.

title: Project, add, and keep the final row
body: W_O combines the heads. The residual keeps E. Only the last updated row feeds this next-token loss.
code:
delta = model.attention.W_O(joined)
updated = E + delta
logits = model.readout(F.relu(model.hidden(updated[:, -1])))

title: The rest of the learning loop is familiar
body: More heads change the context update, not the definition of the next-token target.

title: Score the two observed targets
body: Cross-entropy reads logits and observed token IDs. Do not sample a generated token to make the training target.

title: One loss trains all the projections
body: Heads are not assigned jobs or separate labels. They receive gradients from the same prediction loss.
code:
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

title: Start generation from known token IDs
body: We already encoded the river sentence. A real application tokenizes and looks up a new prompt with the same vocabulary.

title: Generate one token, then repeat
body: At inference, weights stay fixed. The current prefix becomes longer; we keep only the configured context window.
code:
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(history[:, -model.context:])
next_id = logits.argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
history = torch.cat([history, next_id], dim=1)

title: Trace one request through the full model
body: Start at the known IDs. Name the shape at each arrow. Where does the observed target enter during training? It enters only at the loss.

title: The same operation, packaged by PyTorch
body: Which boxes does nn.MultiheadAttention replace?

title: Replace the head calculation, not the whole model
body: The PyTorch layer replaces both heads, their concatenation and W_O. We still add the residual and use our prediction MLP.

title: Create the multi-head attention layer
body: batch_first=True means [B,T,D]. bias=False and dropout=0 match our scratch implementation.
code:
mha = nn.MultiheadAttention(
    embed_dim=4, num_heads=2, bias=False,
    dropout=0.0, batch_first=True)

title: Pass E as query, key and value input
body: PyTorch performs the learned projections internally. average_attn_weights=False preserves the head axis in the returned weight tensor.
code:
delta, A = mha(E, E, E, attn_mask=future,
               average_attn_weights=False)
updated = E + delta

title: Compare the same weights, not two random layers
body: The notebook copies the scratch Q/K/V and W_O parameters into PyTorch, then checks both outputs numerically.
code:
mha = copy_to_pytorch(model.attention)
delta_scratch, A_scratch = model.attention(E)
delta_api, A_api = mha(E, E, E, attn_mask=future,
                      average_attn_weights=False)
torch.testing.assert_close(delta_api, delta_scratch)

title: What the attention block does not include
body: nn.MultiheadAttention does not add position embeddings, the residual, a vocabulary head or a training loop.

title: Do more heads help this experiment?
body: Move from the small worksheet to the actual TinyStories checkpoints.

title: More heads need not mean more parameters
body: Q, K, V and W_O remain 64×64. The number of attention patterns grows, while each pattern uses fewer matching coordinates.

title: Four heads improved held-out prediction here
body: Three-seed means. Same stories, tokenizer, context and update budget; validation-selected checkpoints. Perplexity = exp(cross-entropy). Lower is better. This does not guarantee better text for every prompt.

title: Compare the cost as well as the score
body: Mean training time on Apple M2 Max/MPS, including validation checks. Both attention models have equal parameter counts; the MLP is larger.
